title: Distributed Job Scheduler
prompt: Design a shared service where teams register jobs to run once at a set time or on a cron schedule, and the service makes sure each run happens on time, even when machines fail.

clarify.q: What does a job actually do: call an HTTP endpoint, run a container, or run code on our workers?
clarify.why: If we only call the owner's endpoint, our workers are thin and cheap. Running arbitrary code means sandboxing, resource limits and much bigger workers.

clarify.q: How precise must start times be: within a second, or within a minute?
clarify.why: Second-level precision forces a fast due-time scan and lots of spare capacity at busy moments. Minute-level precision lets us spread load.

clarify.q: Is it acceptable for a run to happen twice, as long as it is rare?
clarify.why: If yes, we can use at-least-once execution with leases. True at-most-once means some runs are silently skipped after a crash, which is usually worse.

clarify.q: What should happen to runs missed while the system was down?
clarify.why: Running all missed runs, only the latest, or none is a per-job policy. It changes how recovery behaves after an outage.

clarify.q: How long do jobs run, and can they be cancelled?
clarify.why: Long jobs need heartbeats so we can tell a slow job from a dead worker. Cancellation needs a way to reach a running worker.

clarify.q: Do jobs depend on each other (run B after A)?
clarify.why: Dependencies turn a scheduler into a workflow engine. It is better to agree that is out of scope or a later layer.

clarify.q: How many jobs, and do many share the same time, like midnight or the top of the hour?
clarify.why: Humans pick round times. The size of that spike, not the daily average, sizes the dispatcher and the workers.

functional: Register a job with a cron expression or a one-off run time, a target, a timeout and a retry policy.
Start each due run within 10 s of its scheduled time at p99, outside known spikes.
Retry failed runs with backoff up to a limit, then move them to a dead-letter list.
Detect a dead worker and give its run to another worker.
Apply a per-job policy for runs missed during an outage: run once, run all, or skip.
Show run history (start, end, attempt, result) per job.
nonFunctional: No scheduled run is ever lost: every due run starts at least once.
Duplicate runs are rare (under 0.01%) and always carry the same run id, so jobs can deduplicate.
99.99% availability for scheduling and dispatch; the API to edit jobs can be 99.9%.
Scale to 100 M runs per day and a spike of over 400,000 runs due in the same second.
One team's flood of jobs cannot delay other teams' jobs by more than a minute.
outOfScope: Dependencies between jobs (a workflow or DAG engine).
Running arbitrary user code in sandboxes; we call the team's endpoint or queue.

assumptions: 10 M recurring job definitions plus one-off jobs: 100 M runs per day in total
10% of daily runs are scheduled at exactly the top of an hour
Average run lasts 30 s; workers handle 50 runs at once each
Workers heartbeat every 10 s while running
A run record is about 300 bytes; history kept for 30 days

steps.label: Top-of-hour spike
steps.math: 10% × 100 M = 10 M per day; 10 M / 24 hours ≈ 416 700 runs due at hh:00:00
steps.result: ≈ 417 k runs due in one second, 360× the average per-second rate

steps.label: Steady worker fleet
steps.math: 1 157 runs/s × 30 s ≈ 34 700 running at once; / 50 per worker ≈ 700 workers

steps.label: Draining the spike with spare capacity
steps.math: 417 k × 30 s = 12.5 M slot-seconds; with 35 k spare slots, 12.5 M / 35 k ≈ 357 s
steps.result: ≈ 6 minutes to work through the spike, so most of those runs start late

steps.label: Heartbeat writes
steps.result: ≈ 3.5 k small lease updates/s, more at the spike

steps.label: Run history storage
steps.result: ≈ 0.9 TB, partitioned by day and dropped after 30 days

estimates.takeaway: The daily average (about 1,160 runs/s) is easy. The design is driven by the top-of-hour spike: 417 k runs due in one second, which would take 6 minutes to drain even with double the steady worker fleet. So we need a dispatcher that can enqueue hundreds of thousands of runs within seconds, sharded by job, and a product rule that jobs which do not need an exact second get spread over a window. Lease heartbeats at ~3.5 k writes/s need a store sized for small, frequent updates.

api.body: { name, schedule: { cron, timezone } | { runAt }, target: { url | queue }, payload, timeoutSec, retry: { max, backoff }, misfirePolicy, jitterSec? }
api.note: Idempotency-Key header so retried registrations do not create duplicate jobs.
Changing the schedule recomputes the next run and removes the old pending one.

api.returns: 200 { runs: [{ runId, scheduledFor, attempt, state, startedAt, endedAt, error }] }

api.note: Workers pull work; the attempt number doubles as a fencing token.

api.path: Worker: Heartbeat(runId, attempt) / Complete(runId, attempt, result)
api.note: Rejected if the attempt is no longer current, so a slow zombie cannot overwrite a newer attempt's result.

entities.name: Job
entities.why: The definition. Only the next occurrence is ever materialised, not a year of future runs.

entities.name: Run
entities.store: Postgres, same shard as its job, partitioned by day
fields: scheduled | queued | running | succeeded | failed | dead
entities.why: One row per occurrence. A deterministic runId means creating the same run twice is a no-op.

entities.name: DueBucket
entities.store: Postgres table per shard (or Redis sorted set)
entities.why: The time-bucketed index the dispatcher scans: 'what is due in this second on this shard'.

data.note: A run's id is jobId + scheduledFor, so the planner can safely try to create the same occurrence again after a crash and the unique key makes it a no-op. Jobs, runs and due buckets for one job live on the same shard (256 logical shards mapped onto a few database nodes), so planning and leasing are single-shard transactions. The due index is ordered by time; at the top-of-hour spike each shard sees about 1,600 runs in one bucket, which is a single indexed range read.

hld.summary:
The API stores job definitions and computes each job's next run time. A planner per shard creates the next Run row and its DueBucket entry a few minutes ahead of time. A dispatcher per shard, owned by one node at a time through a shard lease, wakes every second, reads the bucket for now, marks those runs queued and pushes them onto a ready queue partitioned by team so one team cannot starve others.

Workers pull from the ready queue, claim the run with a lease (attempt + 1, leaseUntil now + 30 s), call the target, heartbeat every 10 s, and complete with their attempt number. A reaper finds runs whose lease expired and requeues them with backoff, or moves them to dead-letter after the retry limit. When a run finishes, the planner creates the next occurrence.

diagram.title: From job definition to a running worker
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  U[Team service] --> API[Job API]
  API --> DB[("Postgres jobs, runs, due buckets")]
  PL[Planner per shard] --> DB
  DS[Dispatcher per shard] --> DB
  DS --> Q["Ready queue by team"]
  W[Worker pool] --> Q
  W -->|claim, heartbeat, complete| DB
  W --> T[Team endpoint or queue]
  RP[Lease reaper] --> DB
  RP --> Q
  CO[Shard coordinator] --> DS

flows.title: A cron job runs at 09:00
steps: At 08:55 the planner creates Run(job, 09:00) with state scheduled and a DueBucket entry for 09:00:00 on that job's shard.
At 09:00:00 the shard's dispatcher reads the bucket, sets the run to queued and publishes it to the team's ready queue partition.
A worker pulls it, claims it (attempt 1, lease until 09:00:31), and calls the team's endpoint with runId as an idempotency key.
It heartbeats every 10 s, then completes with attempt 1; the planner computes and stores the 10:00 run.

flows.title: A worker dies mid-run
steps: At 09:00:31 the lease expires; the reaper sets the run back to queued with nextAttemptAt after backoff.
Another worker claims it as attempt 2 and calls the endpoint with the same runId.
If the first worker was only paused and later calls Complete with attempt 1, it is rejected as stale.

flows.title: Recovering after a 20-minute outage
steps: Dispatchers restart and find buckets from 09:00 to 09:20 not yet processed.
For each job they apply its misfire policy: run_once collapses the missed runs into one, run_all queues each, skip drops them and records skipped.
Catch-up is rate-limited per team so the backlog does not swamp current runs.

deepDives.title: Finding due jobs: time-bucketed queues
deepDives.problem: Every second, we must find all runs due now among millions of future ones, and handle 417 k due in the same second at the top of the hour. Scanning a whole jobs table each second does not work.

options.name: Poll an index on nextRunAt
options.how: SELECT ... WHERE nextRunAt <= now() ORDER BY nextRunAt LIMIT 1000 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, from many pollers.
pros: Simple; one table
SKIP LOCKED lets pollers share work
cons: Hot index on one time column; contention at the spike
Polling cost even when nothing is due

options.name: Redis sorted set per shard
options.how: Score = due time. Dispatcher does ZRANGEBYSCORE up to now, moves members to the ready queue.
pros: Very fast range reads
Natural time ordering
cons: A second source of truth next to the database
Losing Redis data loses runs unless rebuilt from the database

options.name: Per-second buckets per shard in the database
options.how: Planner writes (shard, bucket second, runId). One dispatcher per shard reads exactly one bucket each second and marks it processed.
pros: One small range read per shard per second
Durable; recovery just means reading old unprocessed buckets
Spike spread across 256 shards
cons: Needs shard ownership (leases) for dispatchers
Bucket rows add write volume equal to the run rate

deepDives.choice: Use per-second buckets per shard in the database. At 256 shards the spike is about 1,600 runs per shard-bucket, which one dispatcher can read and enqueue in well under a second. Durability comes for free and catching up after an outage is just reading older buckets. I would add an in-memory timing wheel in each dispatcher, loaded a few minutes ahead, only if second-level precision became a hard product requirement and database reads at the boundary proved too slow.

deepDives.title: Lease-based execution and fencing
deepDives.problem: A worker can die, hang, or pause for a long garbage-collection cycle. We must give its run to someone else, but a paused worker may wake up and report a result after a new attempt has started.

options.name: Queue visibility timeout only
options.how: The run message reappears in the queue if not deleted within N seconds.
pros: No lease logic of our own
Supported by most managed queues
cons: Long jobs need the timeout extended correctly
No fencing: a late worker's result is accepted as if current

options.name: Database lease with attempt number as fencing token
options.how: Claim: UPDATE run SET state='running', attempt=attempt+1, leaseOwner=$w, leaseUntil=now()+30s WHERE runId=$r AND (state='queued' OR (state='running' AND leaseUntil < now())). Heartbeat and Complete include the attempt and are conditional on it still being current.
pros: Clear owner at any moment
Stale workers are rejected, not just ignored
Lease length tunable per job
cons: About 3.5 k heartbeat writes/s
Clock skew between workers and database matters; use database time

deepDives.choice: Use the database lease with a fencing token. Leases are 30 s with 10 s heartbeats, so we tolerate two missed heartbeats before reassigning. All time checks use the database clock, not the worker's. Because the attempt number is passed to the team's endpoint too, a downstream system can also reject writes from an old attempt. If heartbeat volume grew 10×, I would move leases into a dedicated store such as etcd or a Redis cluster with its own fencing counter, keeping the run history in Postgres.

diagram.title: A paused worker loses its lease
diagram.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant W1 as Worker 1
  participant DB as Run store
  participant RP as Reaper
  participant W2 as Worker 2
  W1->>DB: claim run R, attempt 1, lease 30 s
  W1->>DB: heartbeat attempt 1
  Note over W1: long pause, no heartbeats
  RP->>DB: lease expired, requeue R
  W2->>DB: claim run R, attempt 2
  W2->>DB: complete attempt 2, success
  W1->>DB: complete attempt 1
  DB-->>W1: rejected, stale attempt

deepDives.title: At-least-once with idempotent jobs
deepDives.problem: Leases can give a run to a second worker while the first is still working, and a worker can crash after the job's effect happened but before it reported success. So some runs will execute twice. The question is how to make that harmless.

options.name: Aim for at-most-once
options.how: Mark the run done before calling the target; never retry.
pros: Never runs twice
cons: A crash means the run silently never happens
Breaks the 'no run is ever lost' requirement

options.name: At-least-once plus a stable run id
options.how: Always retry until success or the limit; pass runId (jobId + scheduledFor) and attempt to the target, which deduplicates on runId.
pros: Nothing is lost
Duplicates are cheap for the target to detect
The same id survives retries, reassignment and outage recovery
cons: Every job owner must make their handler idempotent
Side effects with no natural key (sending an email) need a dedup table on the team's side

deepDives.choice: Choose at-least-once plus a stable run id, and make it part of the contract: the platform guarantees every run starts at least once and that duplicates share a runId. We help teams with a client library that records processed runIds. For the few jobs where a duplicate is truly harmful and the target cannot dedupe, I would let the job opt into a 'mark started first' mode with the explicit risk of skipped runs, rather than weaken the default.

deepDives.title: Missed runs and the top-of-hour spike
deepDives.problem: Two related problems. After an outage, thousands of jobs have runs that should already have happened. And every hour, 417 k runs are due in the same second, which takes about 6 minutes to drain on the fleet we have.

options.name: Run everything as fast as possible
options.how: On recovery and at spikes, enqueue all due runs immediately.
pros: Simple
Earliest possible start for each run
cons: Floods workers and team endpoints at once
One team's backlog delays everyone else

options.name: Per-job misfire policy and jitter
options.how: Each job chooses run_once, run_all or skip for missed runs, plus an optional jitter window (for example 0–300 s) applied by the planner when choosing the bucket.
pros: Owners decide what makes sense for their job
Jitter flattens the spike before it reaches workers
cons: Owners must understand the options
Jittered jobs start later than written, by design

options.name: Fair queues per team
options.how: Ready queue is partitioned by team; workers pull round-robin with a per-team concurrency cap.
pros: Isolation: one team's 100 k jobs cannot block another's 10
Caps protect team endpoints
cons: Idle capacity may sit unused if caps are too strict
More partitions to manage

deepDives.choice: Combine all three except the first: misfire policies (default run_once, because most recurring jobs only care about the latest state), jitter by default for new jobs that do not ask for an exact second, and fair per-team queues. With a 300 s jitter window, the 417 k spike becomes about 1,400 runs/s, close to normal load. If a large share of jobs really needed second-level precision at the top of the hour, I would pre-scale the worker fleet a minute before each hour rather than keep double capacity all day.

failures: Its shard lease expires in about 10 s; the coordinator gives the shard to another node, which resumes from the last processed bucket; runs start a few seconds late, none are lost.
Heartbeats stop, the lease expires after 30 s, the reaper requeues the run as a new attempt; the run's own timeout also kills it on the worker.
Runs fail and retry with exponential backoff; after the limit they go to dead-letter with an alert to the owning team; a per-team circuit breaker stops wasting worker slots.
The whole scheduler is down for 20 minutes
On restart, dispatchers read the unprocessed buckets and apply each job's misfire policy, rate-limited per team.
Database primary for one shard fails
Promote its replica; dispatch for those 1/N of jobs pauses for under a minute; leases are re-checked against the new primary's clock.
A cron expression is wrong, firing every second instead of every day
Per-job minimum interval and per-team run quotas reject it at registration or pause it with an alert.
scale: 10× runs (1 B/day): about 11,600 runs/s average; increase logical shards to 1,024 and move them onto more database nodes; heartbeats at ~35 k/s go to a separate lease store.
Much longer jobs (hours): leases stay short with heartbeats; add checkpoints so a retried attempt can resume instead of starting over.
Multi-region: each job has a home region that owns its shard; a region failover moves shard leases, and misfire policy handles the gap.

followups.q: How do you handle time zones and daylight saving changes?
answer: Store the cron expression with an IANA time zone and compute the next run in that zone.
On a spring-forward day, a 02:30 run that does not exist runs at the next valid time once; on fall-back, a repeated 01:30 runs once, not twice.
Because runId uses the UTC instant, recomputation cannot create duplicates.

followups.q: How does the planner avoid creating a run twice?
answer: runId is deterministic (jobId + scheduledFor), with a unique key.
Creating the next run and updating job.nextRunAt happen in one transaction on the job's shard.
A retry after a crash hits the unique key and does nothing.

followups.q: How do you cancel a run that is already running?
answer: Set a cancel flag on the run; the next heartbeat response tells the worker to stop.
The worker gets at most one heartbeat interval (10 s) of delay.
Mark the run cancelled so the reaper does not retry it.

followups.q: How would you build dependencies between jobs later?
answer: Keep the scheduler as the trigger layer and add a workflow engine on top that starts child runs when parents complete.
Each step reuses the same lease and idempotency contract.
Do not mix DAG state into the run table; it makes both harder.

mistakes: Sizing for the daily average and missing the top-of-hour spike.
Promising exactly-once execution instead of at-least-once with a stable run id.
Detecting dead workers without fencing, so a paused worker overwrites a newer result.
Materialising a year of future runs for every job instead of only the next one.
Having one global dispatcher that is both a bottleneck and a single point of failure.

mid: Asked how precise start times must be and what to do with missed runs
Stored only the next run per job and computed the following one after each run
Used retries with backoff and a dead-letter list
Explained how a dead worker is detected (heartbeat or timeout)
Defined a run history table with attempt and state
senior: Found the top-of-hour spike in the estimate and designed for it
Used time-bucketed due indexes sharded so each dispatcher reads one bucket per second
Used leases with an attempt number as a fencing token and rejected stale completions
Chose at-least-once and gave targets a stable runId for deduplication
staff: Proposed jitter and fair per-team queues to protect both the platform and team endpoints
Covered time zones and daylight saving without duplicate or lost runs
Planned shard ownership and failover for dispatchers with bounded delay
Named when to split leases into a separate store based on heartbeat volume
